Central Nervous System
Anatomy
Gray and White Matter of Cerebrum

This lesson covers the subcortical gray matter of the cerebrum (the basal nuclei: caudate, lentiform, claustrum and amygdaloid) and the white matter of the cerebrum, which is classified into association, commissural and projection fibres. It describes the corpus callosum and the internal capsule in detail, including their parts, fibre content and arterial supply, and ends with the corona radiata.

Gray Matter of the Cerebrum

Basal Nuclei (Ganglia)

The basal nuclei are large subcortical masses of gray matter located inside the white matter in the basal part of the cerebral hemisphere. They include:

  • Caudate nucleus
  • Lentiform nucleus
  • Amygdaloid body
  • Claustrum

Caudate Nucleus

A large comma-shaped mass of gray matter with a head, body and tail. Its relations are mainly to the thalamus and the lateral ventricle: the thalamus lies medial to the body of the caudate.

PartRelation to the lateral ventricle
HeadFloor of the anterior horn
BodyFloor of the central part
TailRoof of the inferior horn

Antero-inferiorly, the head of the caudate fuses with the putamen (part of the lentiform nucleus).

Lentiform Nucleus

Shaped like a biconvex lens, it has two parts:

  • Putamen: the darker lateral part; fuses antero-inferiorly with the head of the caudate.
  • Globus pallidus: the paler medial part.

Surfaces and relations

  • Lateral surface: related to the claustrum, separated from it by the external capsule.
  • Medial surface: related to the thalamus and the head of the caudate, separated from them by the internal capsule.

Claustrum

A thin sheet of gray matter lateral to the lentiform nucleus, separated from it by the external capsule. Laterally it is related to the extreme capsule.

Amygdaloid Nucleus

A small nucleus at the end of the tail of the caudate nucleus. It is part of the limbic system.

Corpus striatum. The head of the caudate and the lentiform nucleus are separated by fibres of the internal capsule. Across these fibres, bands of gray matter connect the caudate with the putamen (above the site of their fusion). These bands give a striated appearance, hence the name corpus striatum.

White Matter of the Cerebrum

Fibres of the white matter are classified into three types according to the connections they provide.

TypeConnectsExamples
Association fibresDifferent cortical areas in the same hemisphereShort (arcuate) fibres connect adjacent gyri; long fibres connect different lobes, e.g. superior longitudinal fasciculus
Commissural fibresIdentical cortical areas of the two cerebral hemispheresAnterior commissure (connecting the olfactory bulbs) and corpus callosum
Projection fibresCerebral cortex with subcortical centres (corpus striatum, thalamus, brainstem) and spinal cordAscending and descending fibres, e.g. internal capsule

Corpus Callosum

The largest commissure of the brain, connecting the two cerebral hemispheres. It lies in the floor of the median longitudinal cerebral fissure and appears as a C-shaped mass of white fibres on the medial surface of the hemisphere in sagittal section.

Relations

  • Superiorly: anterior cerebral artery, falx cerebri and inferior sagittal sinus.
  • Inferiorly: fornix, septum pellucidum and posterior cerebral artery.

Parts

PartDescription
GenuThick, curved anterior part; its fibres arch forwards into the frontal lobes forming the forceps minor, which connects the frontal lobes together
RostrumThin prolongation from the genu that joins the lamina terminalis
TrunkMiddle elongated part; its fibres extend laterally and downward forming the tapetum of the lateral ventricle
SpleniumEnlarged posterior part; its fibres curve backward into the occipital lobes forming the forceps major

Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery, except the splenium, which is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery.

Internal Capsule

A bundle of projection fibres lying between the thalamus and caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. In horizontal section it is V-shaped, with its concavity directed laterally.

Parts

  • Anterior limb: between the head of the caudate nucleus and the anterior part of the lentiform nucleus.
  • Posterior limb: between the thalamus and the posterior part of the lentiform nucleus.
  • Genu: the bend between the anterior and posterior limbs, with its concavity facing laterally.
  • Retrolentiform part: behind the lentiform nucleus.
  • Sublentiform part: below the lentiform nucleus.

Fibre content and arterial supply

PartFibre contentArterial supply
Anterior limbFronto-pontine fibres; anterior thalamic radiationAnterior cerebral artery; middle cerebral artery
GenuMedial corticobulbar tract; lateral corticobulbar tractMiddle cerebral artery; internal carotid artery (direct branches)
Posterior limbCorticospinal tract; parieto-pontine fibres; fronto-rubral fibres; superior thalamic radiationMiddle cerebral artery; anterior choroidal artery
Retrolentiform partOccipito-pontine fibres; some parieto-pontine fibres; occipito-tectal fibres; posterior thalamic (optic) radiationAnterior choroidal artery
Sublentiform partTemporo-pontine fibres; inferior thalamic (auditory) radiationAnterior choroidal artery

Corona Radiata

Ascending fibres radiate from the internal capsule upwards and outward like a curved fan to reach the cortex, with a similar arrangement for the descending fibres. This fan-like arrangement of fibres is called the corona radiata.

Key Points / Quick Review

Basal nuclei

  • Caudate, lentiform, amygdaloid body and claustrum.
  • Caudate: head (floor of anterior horn), body (floor of central part), tail (roof of inferior horn).
  • Thalamus is medial to the body of the caudate.

Lentiform, claustrum, amygdaloid

  • Lentiform = putamen (dark, lateral) + globus pallidus (pale, medial).
  • Claustrum is separated from the lentiform by the external capsule.
  • Amygdaloid nucleus lies at the end of the caudate tail and belongs to the limbic system.
  • Corpus striatum: striated look from gray bands crossing internal capsule fibres between caudate and putamen.

White matter types

  • Association: same hemisphere (short arcuate, long e.g. superior longitudinal fasciculus).
  • Commissural: between hemispheres (anterior commissure, corpus callosum).
  • Projection: cortex to subcortical centres and spinal cord.

Corpus callosum

  • Genu: forceps minor. Rostrum: joins lamina terminalis. Trunk: tapetum. Splenium: forceps major.
  • Supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, except the splenium (posterior cerebral artery).

Internal capsule

  • V-shaped in horizontal section, concavity lateral; five parts: anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolentiform, sublentiform.
  • Genu: corticobulbar tracts. Posterior limb: corticospinal tract.
  • Retrolentiform: optic radiation. Sublentiform: auditory radiation.

Internal capsule supply and corona radiata

  • Anterior limb: ACA and MCA. Genu: MCA and direct ICA branches. Posterior limb: MCA and anterior choroidal.
  • Retrolentiform and sublentiform: anterior choroidal artery.
  • Corona radiata: fan-like spread of ascending and descending fibres from the internal capsule.
